body.statement: For every \(T\ge4\), \(\mathfrak D_T^{\mathrm{RS}}\cap\mathfrak D_T=\{D_T^{\mathrm{iid}}\}\subsetneq\mathfrak D_T\), and \(D_T^{\mathrm{mir}}\in\mathfrak D_T\setminus\mathfrak D_T^{\mathrm{RS}}\). If \(K=2\), \(q=(1,0)^{\top}\), and \(R_e^2/R_g^2<(T-1)/T\), no Guo--Liang random-switch law that also satisfies global sign symmetry and pairwise orthogonality attains the finite-horizon parity optimum, whereas \(D_T^{\mathrm{mir}}\) does. This separation is for the fixed-path worst-case MSE of \(\widehat\tau\); it does not compare numerical values with Guo and Liang's asymptotic E-optimal OLS criterion.
body.justification: The theorem makes the feasible-class relation and the exact finite regime of nonattainment by the published random-switch family auditable.
body.gap: Guo and Liang restrict their large-horizon E-optimal OLS analysis to stationary homogeneous Markov switching, whereas the parity optimizer uses dependence outside that family and is evaluated by fixed-path moment-estimator MSE.
body.consumer: It tells an N-of-1 designer when enlarging the legal assignment search beyond homogeneous random-switch laws is necessary to realize the exact parity gain.
body.proof_tex:
Let \(D\in\mathfrak D_T^{\mathrm{RS}}\cap\mathfrak D_T\).  If \(\rho_{\mathrm{RS}}+\gamma_{\mathrm{RS}}>0\), stationarity in \(\texttt{ass:stationary-random-switch-law}\) gives
\[
\Pr_D(X_t=1)=\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{RS}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{RS}}+\gamma_{\mathrm{RS}}}.
\]
Global sign symmetry from \(\mathfrak D_T\) makes this probability \(1/2\), so
\(\rho_{\mathrm{RS}}=\gamma_{\mathrm{RS}}=:p\).  The one-step product then satisfies
\[
\mathbb E_D[X_tX_{t+1}]
=\Pr_D(X_{t+1}=X_t)-\Pr_D(X_{t+1}\ne X_t)=1-2p.
\]
Pairwise orthogonality forces this quantity to zero, hence \(p=1/2\).  The transition matrix then has both rows \((1/2,1/2)\), so the path law is \(D_T^{\mathrm{iid}}\).  If instead \(\rho_{\mathrm{RS}}=\gamma_{\mathrm{RS}}=0\), the chain is constant and \(\mathbb E_D[X_tX_{t+1}]=1\), contradicting pairwise orthogonality.  Conversely the independent Rademacher law is the stationary random-switch law with both transition probabilities equal to \(1/2\), and it belongs to \(\mathfrak D_T\).  Therefore
\[
\mathfrak D_T^{\mathrm{RS}}\cap\mathfrak D_T=\{D_T^{\mathrm{iid}}\}.
\]

By \(\texttt{lem:mirrored-law-membership}\), \(D_T^{\mathrm{mir}}\in\mathfrak D_T\), while
\[
\mathbb E_{D_T^{\mathrm{mir}}}[S_T^2]=a_T<T-1
=\mathbb E_{D_T^{\mathrm{iid}}}[S_T^2].
\]
Thus the two laws differ, so the intersection is a strict subset of \(\mathfrak D_T\) and \(D_T^{\mathrm{mir}}\notin\mathfrak D_T^{\mathrm{RS}}\).  Finally, if \(R_e^2/R_g^2<(T-1)/T\), \(\texttt{prop:iid-optimality-threshold}\) says that the only law in the intersection is not minimax, while \(\texttt{thm:lag-one-minimax}\) and \(\texttt{lem:mirrored-law-membership}\) say that the mirrored law is minimax.  Every comparison here is of \(\mathcal R_T\), the fixed-path worst-case mean squared error of the displayed moment estimator; no equality with an asymptotic least-squares information criterion is used.
